transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I’m here because... it’s about my dad’s lab results. For the past year, I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing them, or holding parts of his bloodwork back. 

I'm a phlebotomist, okay? I draw blood for a living, so I know exactly how the system works. Actually, our lab just switched to a new barcode system last month and it has been an absolute nightmare. The scanner never reads the labels right if there’s even a tiny wrinkle on the tube, and I had to tell my supervisor, like, three times that the printer is out of alignment. It prints the patient names slightly off the edge of the sticker. It drives me crazy because I'm a very detail-oriented person. I have to be, you know? When you're dealing with needles. 

But anyway, with my dad... no matter how many doctors or even my own family members tell me his numbers are fine, I know they aren't. The chart in the system does not match what I saw. I know it doesn't. Someone is messing with it, and trying to get anyone to actually look at the discrepancies is just... it’s really wearing me down.
Aside from your concerns about your dad's lab results, have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people don't seem to notice?

Voices? No. No, I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. My hearing is perfectly fine. Actually, it's really sharp, almost too sharp sometimes. 

Like, I can hear the hum of the centrifuge from all the way down the hall at work. Which is incredibly annoying because the new one we got vibrates so much. I told my manager, Linda, about it. I said, Linda, it's not balanced right, it needs to be recalibrated, but she just brushed me off. She's always doing that. Like last week, we had a potluck for one of the nurses who was going on maternity leave, and I spent two hours making this really nice pasta salad—tri-color rotini, black olives, feta cheese, the works—and Linda put my bowl all the way at the back of the breakroom table behind these cheap, store-bought sugar cookies. 

Who puts a homemade side dish behind cookies? It just... it doesn't make any sense to set up a buffet line like that. People should get the real food first, you know? It's just common courtesy. 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, voices. No, definitely not. I don't have anything like that going on.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that clinic staff are altering/hiding her father's lab results) that has persisted for approximately one year. She denies any hallucinations (auditory or visual), and there is no evidence of disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, or negative symptoms consistent with schizophrenia. Her occupational functioning as a phlebotomist appears largely preserved, and her tangential conversational style relates more to circumstantial detail-orientation (job-related complaints about equipment, a social slight at a potluck) rather than formal thought disorder. There is no evidence of mood episode symptoms (mania/depression) to support a mood disorder with psychotic features, and the fixed conviction that her belief is objectively true (rather than intrusive/unwanted) argues against OCD. This pattern of an isolated, well-systematized delusion with preserved functioning and absence of other psychotic or mood symptoms for more than one month is most consistent with Delusional Disorder, persecutory type (F22).
